fabricated and integrated with an mre reactor provided BY our industry partner lunar resources and a full mre demonstration in vacuum will be conducted to produce an aluminum wire. the wire will be characterized in terms of purity, microstructure, and suitability for additive manufacturing applications. while many methods exist to produce metals from regolith, there has been a strong convergence to mre in the past several years. the core reactor subsystem has been demonstrated in a lab environment BY multiple groups, however, lunar resources  mre technology has been proven at commercial scale for the extraction of metals and oxygen. yet, the ability to directly cast the molten materials to other secondary casting process are not AS mature, particularly removing metal products and slag from the reactor and casting them. in addition, end-to-end testing of mre aluminum wire production in a relevant environment has been lacking. the significance of our proposal is that it builds on a proven technology with strong momentum and fills in key gaps to advance TRL. the focus on aluminum is of strong relevance to polar landing sites of the artemis program, applications for wire additive manufacturing, transmission lines, and structural elements, and maturing the technology stack to TRL 6 will position mre to be used in CLPS demonstration missions before potentially being integrated into a propellant pilot plant.

Description: The 2019/2020 australian wildfire season had wide-scale impacts across the southeast of the continent, where SMOKE and haze degraded air quality for many days for millions of people. hemispheric transport of pollution at low and lofted altitudes also occurred, creating an atmospheric signature over new zealand and south america. research has already shown direct and large impacts on the atmosphere, with feedbacks to the climate, biogeochemical cycles and mid-latitude ozone depletion. key objectives of our proposed work are to characterize the atmospheric composition perturbation resulting from the australian 2019/2020 wildfires to determine the full extent of SMOKE impact AS well AS examine how climate variability relates to this unprecedented fire season. we AIM to answer the questions: what was the atmospheric chemistry response to the australian fire emissions? what is the two-way chemistry-climate feedback to the australian 2019/2020 fires? this work will study the australian 2019/2020 fire season using satellite-based measurements from NASA and other agencies and ground-based remote sensing, AS well AS with earth system modeling. satellite measurements are critical for studying atmospheric composition over regional to hemispheric spatial scales. the southern hemisphere has sparse ground-based measurements compared to the northern hemisphere, and extremely limited measurements over the pacific ocean where the fire pollution from the 2019/2020 australian event was transported, making satellite instruments key tools for studying the event. we will use complementary retrievals of carbon monoxide from the satellite-based instruments such AS mopitt (measurements of pollution in the troposphere), mls (microwave limb sounder), and tropomi (tropospheric monitoring instrument) to gain a 3-dimensional mapping of the fire plume extent from regional to hemispheric scales. longer term measurements, such AS from mopitt, will be used to put this event in historical context. other species such AS formaldehyde from tropomi, ozone from omi (ozone monitoring instrument) and tropomi, and aerosol optical depth from modis (moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer) will help determine chemical impacts. ground-based remote sensing measurements from the long-term stations at wollongong, australia, and lauder, new zealand, provide higher time-resolution and will help to evaluate modeling studies. they will also be used to investigate other species involved in chemical evolution, such AS formic acid and ethane, not easily measured from space. a new multiscale modeling capability of the community earth system model will be used to simulate chemistry on an australian regionally-refined grid (~14 km horizontal resolution) simultaneously with global scales (~100 km horizontal resolution). we will test new parameterizations and new chemistry to identify the optimal configuration to represent these wildfires. finally, two-way climate interactions will be investigated: the role of climate variability in driving the severity of the 2019/2020 season will be probed BY building statistical relationships between climate mode indices and atmospheric composition and the impact of fires on climate will be studied with a chemistry-climate model ensemble.

Description: The global ionosphere electric field varies considerably longitudinally and from day-to-day, but the causes of these changes are not well understood. the main processes that produce electric fields include: the neutral wind dynamo the high-latitude electric fields of magnetospheric origin and the penetration of these fields to lower latitudes. interactions between these processes, their longitudinal variability, particularly during geomagnetic storms, produce highly DYNAMIC yet poorly-understood, longitudinal and day-to-day variations in the global electric field. at the low- and equatorial latitudes, the global electric field CAN rapidly raise or lower the ionosphere, and thus help create or suppress plasma instabilities, generate small-scale irregularities that are deleterious to Global Positioning System (GPS) and radio signal propagation. we propose to improve our understanding of the variability of the global electric field and its impact on the mid-, low- latitude and equatorial ionosphere, BY addressing four specific questions: 1) how DO the lower atmosphere TIDES/WAVES and magnetospheric inputs impact the global electric fields during geomagnetically quiet times? 2) how DO the quiet-time global electric fields impact the longitudinal and day-to-day variability of the ionosphere and plasma instability at the mid-, low-, and equatorial latitudes? 3) how DO geomagnetic storms impact the global electric fields? 4) how DO the storm-time global electric fields impact the longitudinal and day-to-day variability of the ionosphere and plasma instability at the mid-, low-, and equatorial latitudes? we will employ the whole atmosphere community climate model with thermosphere and ionosphere extension (waccm-x) to carry out the proposed work. an upper atmospheric model uses empirical or specified lower atmosphere tidal forcing. this impairs the accurate determination of electrodynamic forcing from both below and above. waccm-x treats the whole atmosphere AS an integrated system, and employs realistic electrodynamic forcing from both below and above. periods of geomagnetic activity that are suitable for this study will be identified. waccm-x will be run with, and without, magnetospheric inputs to understand the interplay between the two forcing sources. ionospheric rayleigh-taylor (r-T) instability growth rates will be calculated using model outputs. the waccm-x runs will be compared with data from incoherent scatter radars (isrs), communication/navigation outage forecast system-coupled ion neutral DYNAMIC investigation (c/nofs-cindi), the defense meteorology satellite program (DMSP), constellation observing system for meteorology, ionosphere, and climate (cosmic), and total electron content (tec), to understand longitudinal variations of the ionosphere and plasma instability from mid- to equatorial latitudes. diagnostic analyses will be conducted to understand physical sources that DRIVE this variability. the project team will make the following contributions to the wider team effort. model output and results from the proposed studies, including the calculated r-T instability growth rates, will be made available to all teams. we will attend team meetings and participate in team collaborative tasks. the proposed studies directly address the LWS focused science topic  mid-latitude and equatorial dynamics of the ionosphere- thermosphere system. it also addresses the key science goal #2 outlined in the current NASA decadal survey:  determine the dynamics and coupling of earth s magnetosphere, ionosphere, and atmosphere and their response to SOLAR and terrestrial inputs. furthermore, it is very relevant to interpreting the output from the current NASA flight mission, the Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk (GOLD). Description: Turbulence evolves through highly nonlinear interaction of a broad spectrum of spatial and temporal scales. researchers have developed computational techniques to resolve all, some, or none of these scales and have developed turbulence models to capture the unresolved effects on the resolved scales or the mean flow field. resolving all (direct numerical simulation or dns), while most accurate, CAN require the largest supercomputer for months for relatively simple flows but is the GOLD standard for scale-resolving simulations (srs). modeling all (reynolds-averaged navier-stokes or rans) CAN give results on complicated flows in hours but the prediction has low confidence for important flows like separation from smooth surfaces. intermediate models (e.g., large eddy simulation (les) or detached eddy simulation (des)) resolve larger scales and provide intermediate accuracy and cost. for too long, researchers have pitched a particular model in this spectrum AS the key to improved engineering prediction. this proposal seeks to apply simulations across the entire modeling/resolving spectrum to systematically identify modeling successes and failures. rather than promote a single class of models, each lower fidelity model will be assessed with the next higher fidelity model under matched flow conditions. while the idea of using statistics, budgets, and a priori tests from higher fidelity models to identify failures and improvements to lower fidelity models is not new, the effort proposed herein builds strongly on this prior work together with dramatic advances in massively parallel cfd to apply this approach across an unprecedented range of reynolds numbers, srs models, coordinated flow problems, and boundary conditions. specifically, this work will study an extrusion of a bump profile that matches the centerline coefficient of pressure from a recently started joint computational/experimental study at boeing. BY resolving the wall layer at dns resolution over momentum thickness reynolds numbers ranging from   the tunnel speed (2130), the full tunnel speed (4260), and then up to 25,700 (using dns NEAR the wall and les away from it), wall models for les CAN be tested in a 12-fold rise in reynolds numbers in a combination of zero, favorable, and adverse pressure gradients that occur in rapid succession and result in separation. these conditions replicate the most challenging separated flows on high-lift wing configurations. using these three databases, models will be assessed using a priori and a posteriori closure modeling tests, improved, and then validated on a series of increasingly complex models, including, at the end, application of the improved srs models to high-lift wing configurations. the proposed effort is significant to NASA due to its strong potential to improve both srs models and ultimately rans models. this is important because without improving rans modeling, hybrid models that hold the greatest promise for srs methods will not achieve their full potential.

at this time, msas are the only sufficiently mature technology for space-based multi-object spectroscopy. msas hold several key advantages (e.g. transmissive at all wavelengths, large usable area), however they are expensive and not widely available. an alternative technology to microshutter arrays are digital micromirror devices (dmds): a commercial product, originally developed for the TV and projector market BY texas instruments. dmds consist of a large number of small mirrors (common formats are 768 x 1024 mirrors and 1080 x 2048 mirrors), that CAN be tilted, independently, bi-directionally away from the normal orientation. dmds are a mature, inexpensive, and extremely reliable product. several multi-object spectrographs designed for ground-based telescopes have been built (ritmos, irmos) or are in construction (samos, batman). in previous work, we have shown that dmds are suitable for operation in space. dmds are not particularly sensitive to the radiation environment of space or the mechanical stresses experienced during launch. these devices CAN operate in a vacuum and over a wide temperature range (72 k   400 k). although commercially available dmds are designed for use in the visible regime, we have shown that their use CAN be extended into the nuv range (BY replacing the protective borosilicate window with UV-transparent materials) or the fuv range (BY re-coating the mirror surface with advanced fuv coatings, such AS AL/lif). in this work, we focus on the development of a flight-suitable mos for the FAR Ultraviolet regime, using digital micromirror devices (dmds). the FIRST immediate goal of this work is to build a dmd-based mos for the fuv range and characterize its optical performance. then, we will retrofit this prototype for operation in the nuv/optical range and fly it AS a secondary payload on our sounding rocket, infuse. this would be the FIRST time a dmd-based instrument is flown on a suborbital or space-based platform. this achievement will advance our larger, long-term effort to develop the spectroscopic Ultraviolet multi-object observatory (sumo)   a mission concept with a dmd-based mos AS the primary scientific instrument. in parallel, we will continue our previous efforts to develop coating techniques for the fuv regime, for monolithic optics (mirrors, gratings), AS well AS for more complex segmented optics and opto-mechanical devices. the proposed work leverages the previous successes of several NASA SAT programs aimed at developing dmds for use in space and the development of advanced mirror coatings for the fuv regime. a rigorous characterization of a dmdbased spectrograph in the fuv and a successful demonstration of a dmd-based flight instrument are two critical milestones on the path towards dmd-based instruments for spacebased missions across the full gamut of NASA s mission portfolio.

Description: Gravity wave forcing NEAR the mesopause drives the well-known mesospheric summer-to-winter residual circulation and a reversed, lower thermospheric winter-to-summer residual circulation. the mesospheric residual circulation has been well studied, but the lower thermospheric residual circulation has only come to our attention recently due to its impact on trace species distributions in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere region. recent studies found that the lower thermospheric residual circulation acts like a large eddy that mixes the lower thermosphere, significantly impacting the summer-to-winter latitudinal gradient of thermospheric composition, and thus affecting the ionosphere winter anomaly, AS well AS annual/semiannual variations in the thermosphere and ionosphere (T-i) system. however, these residual circulations are difficult to observe and characterize. also, the gravity wave forcing that drives them is parameterized, somewhat arbitrarily, in general circulation models. it is not clear what the characteristics of the lower thermospheric residual circulation are. it is also not clear how these features change from the solstices to the equinoxes. this undermines our understanding to the variability of composition in the region, and thus limits our understanding of the T-i system and our predictive capability for the system. although the residual circulations are difficult to observe and characterize, they leave clear signatures in trace species distribution. for example, at high latitudes in summer, the upwelling associated with the mesospheric residual circulation increases co2 volume mixing ratio (vmr), whereas the downwelling of the lower thermospheric residual circulation decreases it. this produces a maximum co2 vmr vertical gradient at the transition altitude between the two circulations, and the magnitude of the co2 gradient reflects the convergence intensity. thus, we propose to determine the seasonal variability of the residual circulations from the seasonal variability of tracer distribution. we will address the following specific science questions: 1) where are the top and lower boundaries of the lower thermospheric residual circulation? how DO they vary from the solstices to the equinoxes? 2) how does the convergence intensity at the boundaries of the lower thermospheric residual circulation vary with season? 3) does seasonal variability of the lower thermospheric residual circulation change from year to year? to address these questions, we will use tracer datasets including co2 vmr derived from TIMED-saber (Thermosphere Ionosphere Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics-the sounding of the atmosphere using broadband emission radiometry) observations from 2002-2017, h2o vmr derived from AIM-sofie (aeronomy of ice in the mesosphere-the SOLAR occultation for ice experiment) observations from 2007-2017, AS well AS neutral temperature derived from saber and sofie observations. existing climate simulations BY the ncar waccm (whole atmosphere community climate model) will be used to interpret the data, and the model s capability in representing the characteristics and seasonal variability of the lower thermospheric residual circulation and their effects on TRACERS will be assessed. the proposed study uses datasets from the ongoing NASA heliophysics mission TIMED and AIM. it responds to the NASA hgi program  to maximize the scientific return from operating missions . the proposed investigation address goal #2 of the SOLAR and space physics decadal survey:  determine the dynamics and coupling of earth s magnetosphere, ionosphere, and atmosphere and their response to SOLAR and terrestrial inputs.  the proposed work also address objective h3 outlined in the NASA s heliophysics science and technology roadmap for 2014-2033:  understand the coupling of the earth s magnetosphere-ionosphere-atmosphere system, and its response to external and internal forcing.

Description: Motivation recent discoveries of terrestrial planets orbiting in the habitable zone of nearby stars have energized a number of communities, and increased the urgency of discussions of the criteria for habitability on terrestrial worlds. one potential "show-stopper" for habitability, especially around active m dwarf stars, is the ability of planets to retain an atmosphere when exposed to the photon and particle radiation from their host star. atmospheric escape involves many distinct physical processes that provide energy for atmospheric particles to escape the gravity of their planet. several of these processes involve the removal of charged particles (ions) from atmospheres, and may be particularly important for planets that lack a strong global magnetic field. a number of sophisticated global plasma models have therefore been developed to study atmospheric escape from terrestrial worlds. these models are now well-validated BY observations from planets such AS mars, venus, and titan. but results for the different planets are rarely intercompared, which is an essential step for understanding how loss processes work independent of the planet. a promising path toward a deeper understanding is to use simulations that have been validated BY observations, and then "play with the knobs". objectives our study will focus on how a planet's properties influence the loss of atmospheric particles. we will focus on the loss of charged particles from atmospheres, using models to address four questions: 1. how DO ion escape rates scale with a planet's size? 2. how DO ion escape rates scale with a planet's atmospheric composition? 3. how DO ion escape rates scale with a planet's magnetic field strength (in the weak field limit)? 4. how DO the assumptions of the model (fluid vs. kinetic) influence scaling laws for escape? methodology our work will proceed through application of two well-validated global plasma models for the interaction of the SOLAR wind with unmagnetized planetary atmospheres. the models will be run for identical input conditions corresponding both to our sun and to a "representative" m dwarf star, controlling for a single planetary property at a time. the three planetary properties that will be investigated are the size of the planet, the atmospheric composition, and the planetary magnetic field strength. we will run the models for several choices of each parameter, deriving quantitative scaling laws for ion loss rates for each model. our focus for this research is on ion escape alone, though processes that remove neutral particles are important at some planets. while it is our long term goal to consider both neutral and ion escape in an integrated manner, it would be overly ambitious to propose such an effort here. similarly, we focus our investigation on the influence of planetary properties (rather than external conditions) on ion escape, since this is an unexplored area, is tractable within the period of the award, and has the potential to tell us which kinds of planets are most likely to retain atmospheres. relevance our proposed work probes the ability of terrestrial planets to retain their atmospheres when subjected to photon and particle radiation from their star. the work is theoretical, and focused on the properties of a planet and its atmosphere that result in atmospheric retention. atmospheric retention, in turn, influences the surface habitability of a planet BY controlling the surface pressure and temperature, and influencing whether these quantities are appropriate for the presence of liquid water. the research objectives are not focused on the formation of planetary bodies, the formation of organic molecules, analysis of Spacecraft data, or the evolution of SOLAR system planets. we believe that the work is relevant to the objectives of the Habitable Worlds program, and is not more relevant for any other NASA program.

Description: Accurate mass loss rates are required for astrophysical applications ranging from the evolution of the elements to the dynamics of the interstellar medium. consequently, a firm understanding of the nature of stellar winds and the uncertainties involved in measuring mass loss are essential to many fields. this proposal seeks to apply the sobolev approximation with exact integration (sei) model to repeated observations of ob star wind lines (from the /iue/ and /fuse/ archives), in order to quantify the variability seen in wind line fluxes in physical terms and to investigate its origin. studying these variations is important it two respects. FIRST, changes in the apparent radial optical depth of the wind, determined BY the sei models, is directly proportional to differences in the inferred mass loss rate measured BY any model. consequently, the wind line variability places a limit on the intrinsic accuracy of mass loss rates derived from a single observation of UV wind lines. second, the results will provide clues about the underlying nature of the variability. these CAN be gleaned BY examining the radial dependence of the wind optical depth and how it changes. another important parameter obtained from the fits to doublets is the best fit ratio of oscillator strengths (f-ratio). this parameter CAN be interpreted AS a proxy for the fraction of the line of sight to the photosphere that is covered BY optically thick structures, furnishing important information about the nature of the wind flow. initial results for one series, reveals a relation between the f-ratios and optical depths which, if verified, has important consequences concerning the structure of ob star winds.

Description: The formation of large ice cliffs on tidewater glaciers has a significant impact on ice front retreat, ice flux, and NET mass balance of glacier and ice sheet systems. several large glaciers in the northern antarctic peninsula have in the past few decades exhibited periods of rapid retreat and increased calving, in some cases with ice front cliff heights that approach or exceed modeled thresholds required for rapid cliff ice failure. these changes occurred in the aftermath of ice shelf disintegration events (larsen a and prince gustav in 1995 larsen b in 2002) that resulted from decades of strong climate warming. however, in the past decade, slightly cooler conditions have re-stabilized some of the glaciers, AS persistent m'elange and fast ice at their ice fronts has permitted their readvancement. the antarctic peninsula thus provides examples of the effects of rapidly warming and cooling climatic conditions on a large ice-shelf and its fjord glacier system over a period of several decades. we will analyze the history of the region and provide new insights into a range of ice shelf and glacier processes BY assembling and examining a multi-temporal multi-sensor data set spanning these warming and cooling periods. a primary focus of the study will be the rapid, post-ice-shelf-loss transformations of the ice fronts and lower trunk areas of crane, hektoria-green-evans (hereafter, hektoria), dinsmoorbombardier-edgeworth (hereafter, d-b-e) and r"ohss glaciers. we intend to examine the ice cliff failure process from a primarily observational basis, AS a complement to current model literature on ice cliffs however, model analysis and field work on the processes we infer from the remote sensing observational data will be included. we will use several data sets that have not been previously exploited in this region before. us navy trimetrogon images from the 1960s (figure 4) will be used to generate early surface elevation and flow speed data for the study region. the proposed work will be the focus of a new ph.d. student dissertation, comprising several publications on the region and its wider implications for ice shelf and marine terminating glacier evolution.

Description: The cape floristic region (cfr) of south africa, home to the richest temperate flora in the world, recently experienced its worst recorded drought, with climate projections of continued warming and drying in the coming century. forecasting ecological responses is particularly difficult in the cfr where the challenge is compounded BY extremely high biodiversity, complex ecological feedbacks between recurrent fire and water availability, and pressures of dense human populations. the overarching goal of this project is forecasting how species abundances, community structure, and ecosystem function will respond to climate change. demography is the key AS it provides the lens through which all individual level variation is filtered: individual s traits determine species  demographic rates in different habitats and, ultimately, ecosystem function. major questions that we will address include: 1) when and where are fynbos communities likely to be resilient to change? 2) to what extent will microrefugia ACT AS a buffer against climate change, maintaining existing fynbos communities? 3) to what extent will immigration offset local extinctions, providing resilience in ecosystem function in spite of species composition change? we will establish the mechanistic linkages between fynbos vegetation traits and ecosystem function BY developing a novel approach to community demography that CAN be parameterized with rs data. this will provide a test of recently developed trait driver theory, which synthesizes multiple ecological theories in terms of species' traits. if predictions are accurate, we anticipate that trait driver theory will lay the groundwork for an emerging paradigm in community ecology, biogeography, physiology and global change research. these will be used to provide the FIRST mechanistic forecasts of the future of the cape flora, to understand and manage how a global biodiversity hotspot will change. results will include (1) determining the locations of potential future refugia, (2) mapping species and functional group abundance across the cfr, and (3) understanding how demographic responses will influence ecosystem function and community resilience, in the coming century. in particular, we will determine how much (if at all) fynbos community composition will need to change to track climate change at different types of refugia. this information will be used to guide conservation planning, in particular land management and acquisition priorities for the south african national parks system. we will assess how south africa s current biodiversity monitoring conforms to new essential biodiversity variable standards and use our data and modeled products to bridge gaps. in particular, connecting bioscape and NASA satellite observations finally provides the broad spatial coverage needed to link in situ essential biodiversity variable monitoring to the regional extents needed for conservation planning.

Description: Discovering how communities assemble in novel environments is critical to understanding the evolution of early life and the biosphere. increasingly, observations, experiments, and theory suggest that evolution CAN affect the formation of complex communities. we developed theory on one such DYNAMIC called the monopolization effect. a species monopolizes a system if it arrives early, adapts to novel conditions, and thereby alters the establishment of other species. importantly, monopolization theory suggests that the characteristics of remote ecosystems will depend stochastically on the traits of the FIRST life to evolve or arrive. the extremophile microbes we study are likely analogues for extra-terrestrial life. archaea from the salt extremophile genus haloferax CAN survive the extreme high temperatures (> 50 c) and salty conditions likely found in exposed, low-precipitation planetary environments. our work suggests that these extremophiles CAN adapt quickly to novel conditions, and not just BY mutation: haloferax CAN take up dna directly from other species (horizontal gene transfer) or from the environment, which CAN facilitate their rapid adaptation. thus, a late-arriving colonizer could cheat monopolization BY taking up dna from residents, thus facilitating its adaptation and establishment. key objectives 1) does adaptation of a resident species allow it to monopolize a novel environment and decrease the colonization success of future colonizers? 2) does dna uptake allow a late-arriving species to adapt and establish despite monopolization? 3) how does genetic background and epistasis influence the role of horizontal gene transfer? 4) how DO varying levels of colonization influence community dynamics in multi-patch, linked systems? methods summary we will allow residents (haloferax volcanii) to adapt to novel environments created BY combining different temperatures and salt concentrations. following different periods of adaptation, we will introduce a second species (haloferax mediterranei) adapted to standard conditions. we predict that longer periods of adaptation will enhance monopolization BY h. volcanii. like many early life forms, haloferax CAN exchange genetic material. the resident s adaptations could be passed on to the invader, overcoming the monopolization effect. Description: Dust grains are ubiquitous spatially and temporally within the SOLAR system and in the interstellar medium. spatially, dust CAN be found from the inner through the outer SOLAR system and beyond in the interstellar medium where the composition and physical properties are affected BY the varying temperature and radiation environment. temporally, dust plays a fundamental role in the formation of planetary systems and continues to broadly affect processes from the transport of material on icy moons and saturn s rings to dust storms on mars and levitation/transport of lunar dust. our SOLAR system formed from dust created in a supernova and gases that were PART of a collapsing nebula. most of that material gathered at the center and became our sun. gravity and mass sparked the nuclear fusion that keeps us warm today. explaining everything else remains a challenge. DID the nebula gas accrete onto the dust at different rates depending on the type of gas and the temperature? DID electric charging of the dust and ice BY the young sun s Ultraviolet light contribute to the accretion of gas onto the dust? understanding these basic processes are at the root of answering some of the most fundamental questions posed BY NASA s scientific goal to understand how our SOLAR system formed. today, icy grains of dust are spewed from geysers on enceladus and europa, which affects the surrounding environment. small dust grains in saturn s rings are thought to be charged and therefore transported along magnetic field lines. charged dust grains in martian dust are thought to discharge and produce lightning, which fosters interests in both the science and engineering communities. apollo astronauts noticed a haze above the lunar surface that turned out to be levitated charged dust grains. these processes DRIVE much of the robotic and human exploration in, on, and in between the planets in our SOLAR system. therefore a deeper understanding of the electrical and accretion properties of dust grains is essential from a science and engineering perspective. on the science side these investigations seek to constrain planetary formation and evolution processes and astrophysical processes outside of the SOLAR system. on the engineering side these investigations will help inform instrument, lander, and spacesuit design for dust hazard mitigation in a dusty environment.

Description: Accurate stellar ages constrain a host of astrophysical questions of interest ranging from the habitability of planets to the galaxy's star formation history and age. gyrochronology, an empirical relation between rotation and age, is believed to be competitive with or better than most other methods of stellar age determination for lower main sequence stars. we propose to test competing rotation age models using wide noninteracting binaries. the kepler, k2 and TESS fields contain hundreds of thousands of such pairs. because components of each pair are coeval and share the SAME metallicity, such a large sample offers the opportunity for unique leverage on quantifying what is really a "rotation-metallicity-age relation" for main sequence stars. moreover, wide binaries span a much broader range in age and metallicity than stellar clusters, which may have mixed populations and dynamically lose low mass stars. kepler and TESS are ideal for measuring stellar rotation via modulation of light curves AS active regions (spots) rotate through the line of sight. Description: A large survey of k dwarfs will be carried out to determine the orbital architectures of jovian planetary, brown dwarf, and stellar companions and to characterize the attributes of each star. the k dwarfs targeted are the sun's slightly less-massive cousins that are longer-lived and less variable than g dwarfs, making them excellent hosts for planets with life. the 1217 stars targeted are within 40 pc and lie in a band between declinations +30 and -30, making them observable from major observatories in both hemispheres. two graduate students will lead the efforts on this fundamental sample that will be scrutinized for decades. a key aspect of this work that differs from previous efforts is that *all* stars in a volume-complete sample will be targeted. such a sample is now possible because gaia provides a complete set of k dwarfs out to 40 pc hipparcos was unable to provide this sample because of brightness limits. all stars will be observed uniformly with a single instrument, the chiron spectrograph on the SMARTS 1.5m telescope at ctio. chiron provides spectra at a resolution of 80,000 in slicer mode that are sufficient to extract rvs with precisions of 5--15 m/s for k dwarfs with v  4--12 in 900 sec integrations --- this precision enables the detection of jovian planets. the spectra also allow luminosities, temperatures, metallicities, vsini, activity levels/ages, and accurate space velocities to be derived. because all of the stars are similar in luminosity and temperature, and have datasets from the SAME telescope and instrument, comparisons between stars are straightforward. derived quantities will be combined with photometric variability data from NASA missions and ground-based efforts to provide a dossier on each of the 1217 k dwarfs. the goal is to secure the statistics for orbits out to 3 AU, a distance at which a jupiter orbits a k dwarf in 6 years --- thus, half of the orbit will be covered in the three-year timescale of the proposed work. archival data from chiron will be used to extend the time coverage back to the reopening date of the SMARTS 1.5m in 2017. thus, a subset of the k dwarfs will have up to 8 years of rv coverage, completing orbits for planets at 3 AU and expanding the REAL estate examined for companions. overall, this study will enable the determination of robust statistics for companion populations spanning a factor of at least 800 in mass, from 1 jupiter to 0.8 msun. the ultimate science result will be a three-panel plot showing the orbital period vs. eccentricity distributions for jovian planets, brown dwarfs, and low mass stars across scales similar to our inner SOLAR system. these snapshots will reveal similarities and differences in orbital characteristics that link to the formation scenarios for all three populations. once these stars have been vetted for companions, more powerful techniques CAN explore stars known to have clear inner SOLAR systems for terrestrial planets like earth. this proposal addresses sci-04, sci-07, sci-09, and sci-10 in NASA's exoplanet exploration program's science gap list (2022): sci-04: planetary system architectures: occurrence rates for exoplanets of all sizes --- this work will provide occurrence rates for jovian planets and map orbits, while placing the results within the context of more massive brown dwarf and stellar companions. sci-07: intrinsic properties of known exoplanet host stars --- this work will provide key stellar parameters for more than 1200 of the nearest stars using a single instrument. sci-09: dynamical ation of exoplanet candidates and determination of their masses and orbits --- this work will provide orbits with accurate ephemerides and constrain planetary masses. sci-10: precursor observations of direct imaging targets --- this work will screen for close-in, low-mass stellar and substellar companions.

thermal and energetic plasma environments. the impact of this project would be a substantial improvement in our understanding of the interaction between the pluto-charon system and the SOLAR wind. for understanding of fundamental physics in a unique type of magnetosphere that is occupied BY two bodies of comparable size and, most importantly, that is heavily affected BY ion kinetic effects. besides, we will provide a comprehensive picture of the interconnection between pluto's thermal and energetic plasma environments. this will reveal the mechanisms that LED to several surprising Description: BY combining energetic neutral atom (ena) and magnetic field observations with numerical modeling, this project will analyze the structure and variability of titan's induced magnetosphere during the 126 cassini flybys. in the pre-cassini era, titan's interaction with its magnetospheric environment was usually described in terms of a steady-state draping of the ambient magnetic field around the moon's ionosphere. in particular, the electromagnetic field perturbations caused BY the interaction were treated AS constant during the travel time of the upstream flow through titan's local environment. however, cassini magnetic field and plasma observations from an overwhelming number of titan flybys have revealed the upstream conditions NEAR the moon to undergo significant changes on time scales below one hour. these scales are comparable to the time needed BY titan's induced magnetosphere to adjust to any change in the incident flow conditions and achieve a steady state. so FAR, the deviation of titan's induced magnetosphere from the steady-state draping picture has been constrained only through an empirical analysis of magnetometer data from a subset of flybys. besides, since the magnetic field is sampled only along the Spacecraft trajectory, it contains limited information on the state of the induced magnetosphere AS a whole. for these reasons, we propose to apply ena observations to constrain the impact of ambient magnetospheric variability on the structure of titan's interaction region. enas are generated through charge exchange reactions between energetic magnetospheric ions and neutral particles from titan's atmosphere. therefore, the ena emission morphology is determined BY the trajectories of the energetic parent ions in the draped magnetic fields AS well AS the distributions of uncharged (atmospheric) particles NEAR the moon. thus, the ena images taken BY cassini's inca camera facilitate the characterization of titan's induced magnetosphere AS a whole, thereby greatly amplifying the picture obtained from plasma and magnetic field observations along the trajectory. we will combine the electromagnetic field perturbations from an existing hybrid (kinetic ions, fluid electrons) model of titan's interaction with a particle tracing tool to calculate the trajectories of several billions of energetic parent ions and the resulting ena images observable BY inca. the applied models are based on the notion of steady-state magnetospheric upstream conditions NEAR titan. therefore, a comparison between modeled and observed ena images will reveal any deviations in the structure of titan's induced magnetosphere from the idealized pre-cassini picture. in particular, the locations of regions where the ena emissions are particularly intense or nearly vanish were already found to depend strongly on the magnetospheric field strength and orientation NEAR the moon. we will determine whether the modeled locations and intensities of ena emission maxima and minima coincide with the properties of these features in inca images. such model-data comparisons will be carried out for each subset of cassini flybys that took place under the SAME type of magnetospheric upstream conditions (magnetodisk current sheet, lobe-like, or an admixture of these regimes). in this way, we will determine (i) how strongly the applicability of the steady-state draping picture is affected BY the ambient magnetospheric variability NEAR titan, and (II) whether the characterization of titan's induced magnetosphere based on ena images leads to similar results AS a ``local'' characterization using mag data alone. this project would substantially enhance our understanding of variabilities in titan's induced magnetosphere during the cassini era. in particular, our research would --for the FIRST time-- fully exploit the diagnostic potential of ena images to characterize the moon's induced magnetosphere beyond observations acquired along cassini's trajectory.

Description: The prebiotic formation of sugars, within the context of origins of life scenarios, is both a fundamental and formidable problem that continues to attract possible solutions. historically, attempts to answer the question of the origin of linear sugars has focused on the formose reaction which involves the polymerization of formaldehyde (a c1 sugar) with glycolaldehyde in the presence of calcium ions under highly alkaline conditions. the perceived likelihood of this reaction occurring abiotically has been further enhanced BY observations of formaldehyde in interstellar media suggesting it would be available on the early earth. while the formose reaction has been demonstrated to produce some amount of linear sugars, the utility of the reaction is diminished BY formation of accompanying branched products and tars. even with its many drawbacks, the formose reaction has remained central in the prebiotic formation of sugars. we propose an alternative scenario wherein glyoxylate ( carboxylated formaldehyde ), is utilized AS the primary building block, instead of formaldehyde. it is postulated that through a series of aldol reactions, carbonyl migrations, and decarboxylations, linear sugars and sugar acids CAN be produced avoiding the branched-sugars and tar formation. we term this reaction sequence the  glyoxylose reaction.  broadly, this proposal describes a different approach to the simultaneous formation of linear sugars and sugar acids under plausible prebiotic conditions.

Description: Delays in space/ground communication due to signal latency will present a significant challenge to the collaboration between artemis crews and support personnel on earth. past research examining the impact of signal latency observed that the quality and effectiveness of remote team members' communication suffered irrespective of the delay duration or media (voice or texting). however, this work focused on latencies more characteristic of mars missions than the shorter delays characteristic of lunar exploration. because the delay at the moon will be quite short, space crews and ground support may be inclined to communicate via voice, AS they currently DO in ISS operations. however, a small study of remote collaboration suggests that latencies even AS short AS 3 seconds could degrade the quality of team members' voice communication and impair their ability to maintain common ground -- which is essential for effective communication and perceptions of connectedness between remote team members. the latter aspect seems particularly pertinent in light of research indicating that social relationships between space crew and mission support on earth are critical to their effective collaboration. the AIM of the proposed effort is to explore the viability of voice communication under low signal latencies representative of lunar missions and to examine braiding, a software-delivered text communication tool, AS an alternative to voice communication under these latencies. braiding was specifically designed to facilitate space/ground communication and collaboration and to promote a sense of copresence and connectedness between remote team members despite signal latency. AS a proxy for space/ground collaboration, the proposed work will focus on the private medical conference (PMC), a type of operational conversation that not only has vital health implications for crews during exploration missions, but also requires organized and coherent communication, has measurable performance components and rests on the perception of being engaged in a REAL conversation with a REAL person. the proposed research will involve a human-in-the-loop design used successfully in past research on remote communication. the study will be conducted online with current NASA flight surgeons and will involve two test sessions, about one week apart. pairs of participants will form a space/ground team role-playing a PMC under various signal latencies, using braiding or voice communication dependent on test session. PMC scenarios will be developed with the help of a subject-matter expert and will involve an ambiguous health issue experienced BY the astronaut and requiring diagnosis BY the flight surgeon (md). the participant role-playing the astronaut will receive medically relevant information sufficient for the md participant to identify the underlying cause ( correct diagnosis AS PER scenario design) from several plausible explanations. the study design will enable us to (1) determine whether short latencies undermine the viability and benefits of voice communication during pmcs in contrast to braiding, and (2) compare subjective (e.g., ratings of communication quality and copresence) and objective measures (e.g., communication effectiveness and task performance) of voice vs. braiding for pmcs. it is hypothesized that braiding will be equal to synchronous voice communication on all measures and superior to voice under time delay. the proposed work relates to the expected benefits of braiding AS an effective countermeasure to the risks of communication delays to the functioning of the space/ground team and to crew health during artemis missions. specifically, the work will address hrr gaps team-105--need to identify countermeasures to support team function--and bmed 106--identify effective strategies to maintain personal relations/interactions to mitigate adverse c/p/psy/n outcomes during increasingly earth-independent long duration missions.

Description: The Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) is supported BY the NASA Planetary Defense Coordination Office (PDCO) to operate four 0.5~m telescopes around the world. in 2021, with only two telescopes, ATLAS discovered approximately 1/8 AS many NEAR earth asteroids (NEA) AS the each of the two most prolific surveys, pan-starrs and catalina. the advent of these two new sites at dramatically different latitude and longitude raises an interesting opportunity to develop a better scheduler. currently the ATLAS scheduler simply divides the sky into declination bands and assigns one to each observatory for each night, without regard for weather or the previous night's activity. for most faint asteroids we require four detections (a "quad tracklet") in a night from a single site in order to link them and report them to the Minor Planet Center (MPC) (although bright detections CAN be linked unambiguously with only three). if one of four observations fails (because of clouds for example) we DO not re-queue the observation and quad tracklets cannot be derived from the other three. we make no attempt to link detections between different sites or between nights - this is entirely left up to the MPC. it is possible for a human to command a re-observation of a particularly interesting set of detections, but that is crude and rare. in fact we have a lot of information that is not incorporated into our scheduler. we know with latency less than an hour when a reduction fails so we could usually re-queue it before the night ends or assign it to a different observatory to the west. we have a quantitative, high resolution map of sky transparency from our fisheye observations, so we could avoid observing clouds. we also know what other observatories (not just ATLAS) have observed and intend to observe. we have written a tool (dubbed puma) that links observations between any observatory and at any time which is extremely fast (few millisecond PER linkage) and accurate. the observations from a given observatory night generate ~10^7 difference detections, ~10^9 pairs of detections within an angular velocity limit, from that ~10^6 possible triples, and finally <10^5 quads of which a large fraction are REAL (and known). the false alarm rate for triples is low enough and puma is fast enough that it is possible to link all triples (or a triple and pair) between two nights for an extremely reliable object detection. indeed, at the noise limit the failure to detect an object 4/4 times is a major loss channel. the number of new asteroids grows at about a factor of 6 PER magnitude, so a change of 0.1 mag in linkage sensitivity yields a 20% change in discovery rate. we propose to develop a new scheduler that takes full advantage of the information available about sky conditions, reduction success, and operations at other observatories (including non-ATLAS facilities). further we will develop a module that CAN test interobservatory detections (pairs, triples and quads) to form secure linkages without a consecutive quad tracklet. it this triplet module is sufficiently successful the new scheduler will permit a mode where the normal schedule at a site only visits a field three times (perhaps with longer exposure).

Description: Plasmaspheric hiss WAVES play a critical role in driving particle loss in the inner magnetosphere, yet the origin of these WAVES remains to be fully explained. ray tracing simulations have demonstrated that it is possible for chorus WAVES to propagate up to high latitudes, enter the plasmasphere, and subsequently provide an  embryonic  source of plasmaspheric hiss. modeling efforts have established that chorus WAVES with a specific set of initial conditions, namely a wave vector that is oblique with respect to the background magnetic field (polar angle), and oriented approximately earthwards (azimuthal angle), are crucial to the success of this chorus-tohiss mechanism. however, in the absence of an observationally verified angular distribution of chorus wave power, these results often relied on assumed distributions, typically centered around the background magnetic field direction with a relatively broad angular width. hartley et AL., [2019] used van allen probes observations to determine the angular distribution of chorus WAVES, finding that this distribution is peaked in the anti-earthwards direction, with very few occurrences in which the wave vector is oriented azimuthally earthwards. this study also revealed that the high planarity of chorus WAVES implies a substantially narrower angular distribution than has been assumed in previous work. these two key findings imply that, in general, the amount of chorus wave power that CAN ACCESS the plasmasphere may be substantially less than previously modelled. the exception to this is when the chorus source is located in the vicinity of a plasmaspheric plume. from source locations on the edge of plumes it was found that a large fraction of chorus WAVES CAN propagate into the plasmasphere and potentially evolve into plasmaspheric hiss. this recent publication directly identified chorus sources located in the vicinity of plumes AS a necessary criterion if a substantial fraction of chorus wave power is to propagate into the plasmasphere and become a source of plasmaspheric hiss. AS such, direct investigation of chorus WAVES in the vicinity of plasmaspheric plumes is crucial to determining the coupling mechanism between chorus and hiss. no such studies have taken place, and the variation of chorus wave properties and propagation characteristics in the vicinity of plasmaspheric plumes have not been directly evaluated. the proposed work will directly address this subject area through a dual approach of analyzing the extensive van allen probes data, coupled with ray tracing simulations. the primary science objective of this proposal is to determine the angular distribution and propagation characteristics of chorus WAVES in the vicinity of plasmaspheric plumes and directly evaluate their impact on the plasmaspheric hiss wave population. to DO this, the following questions will be answered: -- what are the characteristics of the angular distribution of chorus WAVES in the vicinity of plasmaspheric plumes, and how does this distribution vary with separation distance from the plume? -- what initial conditions are required for chorus WAVES to propagate into the plasmasphere from sources located close to plasmapsheric plumes, and how DO these conditions vary for different plume structures? -- CAN the angular distribution of plasmaspheric hiss in/NEAR plumes be explained BY using chorus AS a source? this proposal directly addresses the 2013-2022 decadal survey in SOLAR and space physics scientific goal to  determine the dynamics and coupling of earth s magnetosphere, ionosphere, and atmosphere and their response to SOLAR and terrestrial inputs , in addition to the 2014 NASA strategic plan objective to,  understand the sun and its interactions with earth and the SOLAR system, including space weather.

Description: This three year proposal will support the development, optimization, and testing of chimera - a hybrid magnetometer that simultaneously operates AS both a search coil and a fluxgate. chimera is expected to provide reasonable sensitivity from DC to 10 khz from a single, compact sensor requiring only one deployable boom. this is particularly useful for small Spacecraft and cubesats, where multiple deployable booms are challenging so even modest sensitivity over this broad range is significant. the hybrid design builds on established fluxgate and search coil technology with decades of heritage operating in extreme and hostile environments. chimera is aligned with the NASA technology roadmap in technology area 8.3.3 in situ - instruments and sensors and will advance from TRL-3 (Technology Readiness Level) to TRL-6. science missions have often needed a Search Coil Magnetometer for high frequencies and a fluxgate for the static field and low frequencies. these two instruments interfere with each other - the search coil detecting the DRIVE signal from the fluxgate and the ferromagnetic core providing magnetic gain in a search coil distorting the field measured BY the fluxgate. the two resulting deployable booms affect Spacecraft control and CAN impinge the field of view of other instruments. a proof-of-concept laboratory prototype of chimera has demonstrated how to operate a racetrack fluxgate sensor AS both a fluxgate and a Search Coil Magnetometer using essentially the SAME hardware already present in a typical fluxgate instrument. the two sensing techniques CAN operate simultaneously without interfering in a hybrid sensor engineered to accommodate both effects. the proposed project supports early career development for the PI, david m. miles, and higher education training for one graduate student and three undergraduate research assistants. a flight-ready hybrid magnetometer enables the investigation of multiple science questions under the NASA heliophysics overarching science goal to:  advance our understanding of the connections between the sun, earth, the planetary space environments, and the outer reaches of our SOLAR system . a hybrid magnetometer is ideally suited for future missions including: a constellation follow-on to the recent funded gtosat radiation belt cubesat, daughter payloads deployed from the Geospace Dynamics Constellation (GDC), or small ride along Spacecraft that have been suggested for future planetary missions. magnetic field data from DC   10 khz from these missions would be important in addressing, respectively, three science goals identified in SOLAR and space physics: a science for a technological society: swmi science goal 4. establish how energetic particles are accelerated, transported, and lost swmi science goal 7. determine how magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere coupling controls system-level dynamics and swmi science goal 8. identify the structures, dynamics, and linkages in other planetary magnetospheric systems. we have defined three investigation objectives to ensure that the hybrid magnetometer developed under this proposal is suitable for the broad spectrum of future heliophysics missions which require magnetic field measurements. 1) EXPAND the DC   2 khz bandwidth of the current hybrid magnetometer prototype to provide magnetic field measurements from DC   10 khz from a single magnetometer sensor. 2) optimize the search coil action of the hybrid magnetometer to achieve noise and sensitivity within a factor of four of that achieved BY comparably sized traditional search coil sensors (e.g., rbsp, THEMIS) 3) scale down the hybrid magnetometer sensor to nanosatellite geometry (< 10 x 10 x 10 CM^3) while preserving scientifically useful sensitivity from DC-10 khz. chimera will enable high fidelity magnetic field studies on future smallsat/cubesat heliophysics missions around the earth, the moon, and other planetary bodies.

Description: Dormant bacterial endospores are one of the toughest Biological structures on earth designed for survival during unfavorable conditions. contamination of Spacecraft surfaces with endospores has been a long-standing concern related to planetary protection and many studies have been conducted in the past two decades to isolate spore-forming bacteria from surfaces within NASA aerospace facilities and test the survivability of endospores in conditions simulating space and extraterrestrial environments. most of these studies used aerobic bacilli AS model organisms, likely because of well-defined cultivation strategies easy to optimize in and outside of laboratory. furthermore, NASA s standard spore assay also only uses aerobic growth conditions for isolating spore-forming bacteria. members of clostridia, consisting of strictly anaerobic spore-forming bacteria many of which are extremophiles, however, have received much less attention regarding planetary protection. endospores of clostridia were recently shown to be transported via fluid migration and sediment burial and colonize pristine habitats within the earth s subsurface. this project will partner with the astromaterials research and exploration science division at NASA s Johnson Space Center to address two objectives   1) isolation and enrichment of anaerobic, spore-forming clostridia from clean lab samples using anoxic cultivation assays using a combination of different media and incubation temperatures and 2) physiological and molecular characterization of enrichment cultures / isolates using a combination of growth assays and high-throughput dna sequencing. our long-term goal is to help EXPAND NASA s toolbox on identifying and eliminating endospores of metabolically diverse bacteria in aerospace facilities AS potential terrestrial contaminants on mars during future crewed missions.

worlds are hypothesized to be common amongst exoplanets which are now becoming realistic targets for study. molten and recently solidified lava provide views of the magmatic system free of the influences of erosion, weathering, or burial from regolith, and thus are the best candidates for pinpointing the conditions of magma genesis, storage, and eruption drivers in volcanic systems with upward-moving eas sourced from neutrino interactions within the earth have unique sensitivity to the astrophysical and the cosmogenic neutrino flux. for the optical cherenkov signals, the neutrino Description: In the giant impact theory the moon formed in the aftermath of an off-center collision between a planetary sized body and the proto-earth. the collision lofts a ring of debris into orbit around the earth, and this proto-lunar disk then cools and coalesces to form the moon. in the canonical giant impact models (see canup 2004) the impactor mass is comparable to mars and the angular momentum of the earth-moon system is conserved. this models suffers from an "isotope crisis" (e.g. melosh 2014): the moon and earth are isotopically similar, which is unexpected since the moon should contain a material from an impactor that likely originated elsewhere in the SOLAR system. in noncanonical models (cuk & stewart 2012 canup 2012) angular momentum of the earth-moon system is removed via an evection resonance. recent work (lock et AL. 2018) considers high energy and angular momentum impacts in which the collision outcome is a rapidly rotating, well-mixed "synestia". existing giant impact simulations use smoothed particle hydrodynamics techniques or an eulerian grid code with maximum resolution ~ 100km (see canup et AL. 2013). we propose to develop and apply a fast, eulerian scheme based on the athena++ code that is capable of high linear resolution. our code will include the option to evolve an embedded magnetic field in the magnetohydrodynamic (mhd) approximation, motivated BY recent work (gammie et AL. 2016, carballido et AL. 2016) that shows that magnetic fields couple to hot, vaporized parts of the protolunar disk. we propose the following novel investigations of the giant impact hypothesis using numerical experiments: (1) BY what factor CAN a giant impact amplify the magnetic field of the target and impactor? (2) how does a magnetized model differ from an unmagnetized control model? (3) CAN a giant impact remnants lose angular momentum through a magnetized wind? (4) what is the structure (run of density, temperature, composition, and field strength) of the boundary layer between the protolunar disk and earth? (5) what is the rate of mixing through the boundary layer? (6) what is the rate of mixing in a protolunar disk that is in contact with a dynamically active boundary layer? we will answer these questions using a special branch of the athena++ astrophysical mhd code that we will build, test, and publicly release. we hope to create a tool that is useful to communities interested in moon formation, giant impacts, exoplanet formation, and other impact problems that CAN be treated in a fluid approximation. the PI has a record of developing and publicly releasing codes that are widely used in other contexts. the athena++ code is a rigorously tested, highly optimized framework for simulating astrophysical fluids. it is fully vectorized and therefore fast in scalar mode, and it also scales efficiently to hundreds of thousands of cores. this will enable numerical investigation at higher resolution than heretofore possible. we have added tabular equation of state capability to the athena++ code, and are in the process of adding material tracking capability. the work will constitute the phd thesis of illinois graduate student patrick mullen. PI gammie has extensive experience with numerical methods, astrophysical fluids, and disk dynamics. form NRESS-300 version 3.0 apr 09 the proposed work is within the scope of the program element because "emerging worlds" aims to discover how the SOLAR system formed and evolved, and this year the planetary science division is particularly soliciting proposals that focus on the moon.

Description: *objective* the proposal would use topographic data collected BY the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and kaguya Spacecraft AS constraints on the morphology of lunar craters across a large range of size scales, ranging from small simple craters, through the simple-to-complex transition, and up to multiring basins. the proposed work would: 1) collect a set of high quality digital elevation models of the freshest examples of craters of different morphological classes 2) use lunar topography data to quantify the statistical distribution of the morphological characteristics of the craters identified in 1 3) develop efficient, high performance algorithms that CAN simulate the three dimensional morphology of lunar craters that mimic the observed craters and 4) apply the new topographic models to simulations of heavily cratered lunar terrains in order to investigate long-standing problems in lunar crater science, such AS the question of whether or not the lunar highlands are in a state of crater count equilibrium. the new crater morphology models would be incorporated into the cratered terrain evolution model (ctem), a monte carlo landscape evolution model has been used in a number of recent projects aimed at understanding important processes in cratering. an ancillary goal of the study would be to release a public version of ctem BY the end of the study period. *methods* the FIRST task of the proposed study would be to collect a set of  type example  craters for each of the morphological classes that the proposal would model (e.g. simple, simple-to-complex transition, complex, and multiring basin). these type example craters would present minimal degradation and subsequent crater overlap, show prominent ejecta blanket features, and have high quality topographic data available. for each type example, topographic data would be used to generate digital elevation models of the crater and surrounding proximal ejecta region. in the second task, a set of morphological  characters  will be identified and measured. these characters are morphological features of the craters, such AS rim shape, textures of floors, rim walls, and ejecta, rim terrace sizes and shapes, central peak and peak ring sizes and shapes, ETC. the dems would be analyzed using a set of python scripts in order to extract measurements of each of the crater characters for individual craters and calculate statistical variability between craters of a given class. in the third task, algorithms will be developed that CAN reproduce each of the identified crater morphological characters and their observed statistical variations. these algorithms will be primarily derived from a technique called perlin noise, which is a well-established, high performance algorithm developed for computer graphics. in the final task, the new morphology algorithms would be incorporated into the cratered terrain evolution model. once tested and verified, the model would be used to re-investigate the open question of whether or not the lunar highlands are in a state of crater equilibrium. the proposal would re-visit earlier work BY minton et AL. (2015) and riedel et AL. (2020) that used ctem to investigate crater size distributions and crater degradation in heavily cratered lunar highlands using the code s current crater morphology model which does not reproduce realistic complex craters and basins. *significance* from the lunar data analysis solicitation, one of the overall objectives of the program are to  enhance the scientific return of lunar missions.  the available lunar topographic data contains abundant untapped potential to further our understanding of the morphology of lunar craters. the development of realistic crater morphology, constrained BY lunar data, in the ctem code will greatly enhance the utility of the code in understanding the bombardment history of lunar surfaces.

Description: The FIRST objective of this proposal is to determine the radiative properties   scattering and polarization of scattered light AS a function of angle - for a set of proposed sub-neptune cloud analogs in the laboratory. to accomplish this, we will measure the light scattering properties of single, levitated cloud analogs in an exoplanet electrodynamic balance (exoedb) designed for studies under exoplanetary atmospheric conditions. in conjunction we will measure the light scattering properties for a continuous bulk flow (or ensemble) of cloud analogs with a measured particle size distribution and compare these to the single particle measurements. both systems are equipped with identical optical components and discrete wavelengths of illumination. thus, using both systems to measure the scattering properties of the SAME cloud analogs we will gain a deep understanding of how the signatures of scattering and polarization of scattered light are affected BY multiple scattering from neighboring particles within a cloud layer, and how this will impact observations and model outcomes. finally, we will build a publicly accessible, online database of collected laboratory data for use BY the exoplanet modeling and observational communities. to complete our understanding of clouds in sub-neptune atmospheres we have broken the second objective into two parts: integrating laboratory derived scattering data into the community aerosol and radiation model for atmospheres (carma) and using laboratory derived data to model planetary geometric albedo spectra and optical phase curves with the planetary intensity code for atmospheric scattering observations (picaso). the FIRST PART aims to improve the ability of carma to model interactions between atmospheric particles and stellar radiation through parameterizations based on how sub-neptune cloud analogs scatter light in the laboratory. the second PART aims to discover unique insights into particle properties that CAN be derived from optical phase curves - stellar light scattered BY the planet towards the observer AS a function of its location in its orbit - given laboratory scattering phase functions. AS such we will develop theoretical and observational constraints, useful for the detection and characterization of exoplanet atmospheric properties, informed BY our physical findings. this dual approach, combining laboratory and theoretical work, has the potential to greatly EXPAND our understanding of Particulate Matter in exoplanet atmospheres, and may ACT AS a stepping-stone towards polarization measurements BY space-based telescopes for exoplanet characterization. this proposal addresses several points of the xrp call: it will contain basic research focused on the understanding of exoplanets, explore the chemical and physical properties of exoplanet atmospheres, aid in the observational characterization of exoplanets, and has the potential to significantly improve our understanding of exoplanets systems through combined laboratory and theoretical studies.

Description: Only one history of life has been recorded on our planet, and much of this history is resolved at the organismal population level. in a critical sense, though, it may be argued that the essential Biological intermediates that drove global geochemical cycles in the earth s deep history were not organismal but metabolic, driven BY the presence and behavior of key enzymes in microorganisms. how DID these key metabolisms evolve? CAN we reconstruct the contributing metabolic factors of this Biological past? this proposal aims to reconstruct key enzymatic intermediates between Biological activity and global geochemical reservoirs throughout earth's deep history, specifically nitrogenase enzymes. nitrogen is a critical nutrient for all living organisms, yet, the deep history of the global nitrogen cycle is notoriously obscure. nitrogen cycling has been biologically controlled for billions of years, but we still DO not know when organisms FIRST began pulling nitrogen from the air (a process called nitrogen fixation), in what sort of environment nitrogen metabolism evolved, or how the earliest nitrogen-fixing enzymes functioned. our interpretations of the chemical traces left BY ancient metabolic processes have been in terms of our knowledge of modern enzymes. here a computation and experimental research proposal is presented to reconstruct ancient nitrogen-fixing proteins to interpret the nitrogen record in geologic time. specifically, tools drawn from phylogenetics, molecular and systems evolution, biochemistry and geobiology will be utilized to travel backwards in evolutionary time in the laboratory. we will follow the evolutionary history of microbial dna to assess the possible environmental impacts of ancient enzymes on global-scale signatures that record Biological activity.

Description: The inductive generation of a global magnetic field BY the motion of conducting fluid in a planetary core is known AS the dynamo. although the moon today has no global magnetic field, recent paleomagnetic measurements of apollo samples indicate that the moon generated a dynamo from at least 4.25 to 1.92 billion years ago (ga). furthermore, sample measurements suggest that prior to about 3.5 ga, a putative high-field epoch  existed when the field intensity may have reached ~70 microteslas (ut) (earth-strength). however, because metallic minerals in lunar samples alter when heated in air, nearly all previous paleointensity determinations from samples older than ~3.3 ga have employed non-heating techniques, which have uncertainties ranging up to an order of magnitude or more for some samples. dynamo scaling laws indicate that if the moon s dynamo were generated BY convection in the core, its surface field should not have continuously exceeded ~10 ut over the period 4.2-3.5 ga. therefore, if the field indeed continuously reached such values of > 70 ut AS tentatively suggested BY existing data, then two possible explanations are (i) the lunar core generated a convective dynamo but one that only intermittently reached such high fields during this period or (II) the lunar dynamo was driven BY a process other than core convection that was capable of continuously producing stronger fields. alternatively, (III) the high apparent paleointensities are in error and the field never actually exceed 10 ut. any of these 3 outcomes would have major implications for our understanding of the moon s origin, thermal history, interior structure, orbital history, and the physics of dynamo generation. the key to resolving this issue is to obtain accurate (<10% uncertainty) paleointensities. such accuracies could be obtained if laboratory heating could be conducted without altering the samples. with this goal, we recently developed a controlled-oxygen fugacity thermal demagnetization system. furthermore, we have recently recognized that glassy lunar regolith breccias have optimal magnetic recording properties due to the fine sizes of their constituent metal grains. applying this controlled atmosphere heating apparatus to three regolith breccias, we have recently obtained the FIRST accurate heating-based lunar paleointensities for the period after 2 ga. here we propose to constrain the intensity of the early lunar dynamo and  or refute the existence of a high-field (i.e., tens of ut) epoch using controlled-atmosphere thermal paleointensity analyses. we will analyze four glassy lunar breccias older than 3.4 ga that are likely to have high-fidelity records of the global lunar field spanning >0.2 billion years of history. we will conduct this work AS PART of two tasks: task 1. measure the paleointensity of the lunar field using paleomagnetic analyses task 2. constrain the ages of the paleointensities using AR-based geochronometry. if we find that the lunar field over the period ~3.4-4.9 ga was either continuously present but weaker than ~10 ut, or else greater than 10 ut but only intermittently, then this would indicate that the early dynamo could have been generated BY core convection [outcome (i) above]. alternatively, if we find that the dynamo surface field was continuously stronger than ~10 ut over this period, this would suggest that the dynamo was generated BY a process other than core convection [outcome (II)]. finally, if we find (III) that all paleointensities during this period are actually weaker than ~10 ut, then this would be compatible with a continuously operating core convection dynamo.
